text: In this novel, a pig named Wilbur is saved from the butcher when a spider spins words such as "Some Pig" and "Radiant" into her web. The girl Fern first rescues Wilbur as a runt, and he later wins a special prize at the county fair. For 10 points, name this E. B. White children's book named for its spider.

The Sorting Hat places students into houses such as Gryffindor and Slytherin at this school, where Hagrid is gamekeeper and Albus Dumbledore is headmaster. Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley are friends of the title character of the series set there. For 10 points, name this British author of the Harry Potter books.

Friar Laurence marries the two title characters in secret, and a feud between the Montagues and the Capulets ends in tragedy when Tybalt kills Mercutio. A famous scene takes place on a balcony, and both lovers die in a tomb. For 10 points, name this play by William Shakespeare set in Verona.

In this novella, the ghost of Jacob Marley warns a miser that he will be visited by three spirits. The spirits show him his lonely past, his clerk Bob Cratchit's family, and the sickly Tiny Tim. For 10 points, name this Charles Dickens story about Ebenezer Scrooge, set at the holiday it names.

In this epic poem, the hero blinds the Cyclops Polyphemus, resists the song of the Sirens, and is delayed for years by the enchantress Circe. After ten years of wandering, he returns to Ithaca and defeats the suitors of his wife Penelope. For 10 points, name this epic attributed to Homer, a sequel of sorts to the Iliad.

This author, whose real name was Theodor Geisel, wrote "The Lorax" and "Green Eggs and Ham." His rhyming books feature a mischievous cat in a striped hat and a grumpy creature who tries to steal Christmas. For 10 points, name this author of "The Cat in the Hat" who used a pen name.

This man served as the third president and doubled the size of the country with the Louisiana Purchase. He lived at Monticello and founded the University of Virginia. For 10 points, name this man who was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence.

The archaeologist Howard Carter discovered this ruler's nearly intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. Found inside were a famous golden funeral mask and a nested set of coffins. For 10 points, name this young Egyptian pharaoh of the 18th dynasty, nicknamed "King ___."

This 1773 protest was organized by the Sons of Liberty in response to the Tea Act. Men disguised as Mohawks boarded three ships and threw 342 chests of tea into the water. For 10 points, name this event in a Massachusetts harbor that helped lead to the American Revolution.

Born Araminta Ross in Maryland, this woman escaped slavery and made about thirteen trips back to the South. She guided enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad and was called "Moses." For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

This man crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, defeated Pompey, and became dictator of Rome. He formed the First Triumvirate with Crassus and Pompey and wrote about his campaigns in Gaul. For 10 points, name this man stabbed by senators including Brutus on the Ides of March in 44 BC.

This period began with the stock market crash of October 1929. Dust storms ruined farms in the Plains, banks failed, and about a quarter of Americans were out of work. For 10 points, name this decade-long economic downturn that led to the New Deal.

Heat from the Sun drives evaporation in this process, and water vapor then condenses into clouds. It falls as rain or snow and flows back to the oceans through rivers and groundwater. For 10 points, name this cycle that moves water between the sky, land, and sea.

This man's "Principia" laid out the laws of motion and universal gravitation. He invented calculus independently of Leibniz and showed that white light is made of many colors. For 10 points, name this English scientist who, according to legend, was inspired by a falling apple.

This Russian chemist arranged the elements by atomic weight and left gaps for undiscovered ones such as gallium and germanium. He published his table in 1869. For 10 points, name this man who created the periodic table.

Galileo discovered four large moons of this planet: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. A storm larger than Earth, called the Great Red Spot, rages in its atmosphere. For 10 points, name this largest planet of the Solar System.

Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in this single landmass, whose name means "all land." It split into Laurasia and Gondwana about 200 million years ago. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent.

This bone is the strongest and the longest in the human body. It runs from the hip to the knee and is protected by large muscles including the quadriceps. For 10 points, name this bone of the upper leg, also called the thigh bone.

Archimedes approximated this number using polygons inscribed in and circumscribed about a circle. It is irrational, so its decimal expansion never ends or repeats. For 10 points, name this number, about 3.14, equal to a circle's circumference divided by its diameter.

This artist's notebooks include designs for flying machines and a drawing of a man with outstretched arms in a circle and square called the Vitruvian Man. He also painted "The Last Supper." For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist who painted the Mona Lisa.

This composer continued to write music after becoming almost completely deaf. His Fifth Symphony opens with four notes that go "da da da DUM," and his Ninth Symphony includes the "Ode to Joy." For 10 points, name this German composer of the "Moonlight Sonata."

This Spanish painter went through a Blue Period and later co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque. His huge anti-war mural shows the bombing of a Basque town. For 10 points, name this artist of "Guernica."

This composer was a child prodigy who toured Europe's courts as a boy with his sister Nannerl. He was born in Salzburg and wrote "Eine kleine Nachtmusik" and an unfinished Requiem. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer of "The Magic Flute."

This fisherman was called Simon before Jesus renamed him, and he walked on water briefly before sinking. He denied Jesus three times before the rooster crowed. For 10 points, name this apostle regarded by Catholics as the first pope.

Its followers observe the Five Pillars, including fasting during Ramadan and making a pilgrimage to Mecca known as the hajj. Its holy book is the Quran, which it holds was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. For 10 points, name this monotheistic religion, whose followers are called Muslims.

This god wields the hammer Mjolnir and drives a chariot pulled by two goats. He fights the world serpent Jormungandr, and the day Thursday is named for him. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, a son of Odin.

According to Hesiod, Hephaestus molded this first woman from clay on the orders of Zeus. She was given a jar, or box, that she opened, releasing evils into the world and leaving only hope inside. For 10 points, name this woman of Greek myth.

This man asked probing questions in a method named for him and was the teacher of Plato. He was tried in Athens for corrupting the young and impiety. For 10 points, name this philosopher who was sentenced to die by drinking hemlock.

This Austrian founded psychoanalysis and described the id, the ego, and the superego. He wrote "The Interpretation of Dreams" and developed the practice of free association. For 10 points, name this psychologist from Vienna.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit of this mountain in 1953. It sits in the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and Tibet. For 10 points, name this tallest mountain above sea level in the world.

The Colorado River carved this landform over millions of years, exposing layers of rock up to a mile deep. It is in Arizona and is roughly 277 miles long. For 10 points, name this enormous canyon, a national park and a popular destination for rafters.
Computers use this number system because transistors have two states, on and off. A single digit in it is called a bit. For 10 points, name this base-two system that uses only the digits 0 and 1.

Johannes Gutenberg introduced this machine to Europe around 1440. It used movable metal type, and its first major product was a Bible. For 10 points, name this invention that made books much cheaper to produce.

text: In this novel, Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth rewriting records and is later tortured in Room 101. The Party uses Newspeak and telescreens, and its leader is the face on posters that say he is watching. For 10 points, name this George Orwell dystopian novel named for a year.

Thornfield Hall is the setting for much of this novel, in which a governess is hired to teach a girl named Adèle. She later discovers that her employer, Mr. Rochester, has hidden his first wife Bertha Mason in the attic. For 10 points, name this Charlotte Brontë novel named for its title heroine.

Hester Prynne is forced to wear an embroidered "A" in this novel, and the minister Arthur Dimmesdale is the secret father of her daughter Pearl. Her husband takes the name Roger Chillingworth. For 10 points, name this Nathaniel Hawthorne novel set in Puritan Boston.

A group of schoolboys is stranded on a deserted island in this novel, where they use a conch to call meetings. The boy Piggy is killed, and the hunter Jack rebels against the elected leader Ralph. For 10 points, name this William Golding novel.

The explorer Robert Walton relays the story of Victor in this novel, which Mary Shelley began during a ghost-story contest in Geneva. Victor brings a creature to life and then abandons it. For 10 points, name this novel whose title is often wrongly given to the monster.

This poet lived in Amherst, Massachusetts, and published very few poems during her life. Her poems use dashes and slant rhyme, as in "Because I could not stop for Death." For 10 points, name this reclusive American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems were found after she died in 1886.

The wrath of Achilles after his quarrel with Agamemnon is the central subject of this epic. Patroclus is killed wearing Achilles' armor, and Achilles then kills Hector. For 10 points, name this Homeric epic of the Trojan War.

King John was forced to accept this document at Runnymede in 1215 by rebellious barons. It limited royal power and promised that no free man could be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers. For 10 points, name this English charter.

Crowds searching for gunpowder and prisoners attacked this Paris fortress and prison on July 14, 1789. The governor, Bernard de Launay, was killed. For 10 points, name this building whose storming marks the start of the French Revolution.

This Venetian merchant traveled to China with his father and uncle and served at the court of Kublai Khan. His account of his journeys was dictated to Rustichello da Pisa. For 10 points, name this explorer, author of "The Travels."

John F. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of an island after U-2 planes photographed missile sites there. Nikita Khrushchev eventually agreed to remove the missiles in October 1962. For 10 points, name this Cold War confrontation named for the country where the missiles were placed.

James Watt's improvements to the steam engine and the invention of the spinning jenny by James Hargreaves were important in this period. It began in Britain in the late 1700s and moved work from farms and workshops to factories. For 10 points, name this era of mechanization.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized this 1848 meeting in New York, where a Declaration of Sentiments called for women's right to vote. For 10 points, name this first women's rights convention, held in a town in the Finger Lakes region.

This man was tutored by Aristotle and succeeded his father Philip II as king of Macedon. He defeated Darius III at Gaugamela and rode a horse named Bucephalus. For 10 points, name this conqueror who died in Babylon in 323 BC after building a huge empire.

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon are the members of this group. They sit in the far-right column of the periodic table and are chemically unreactive because their outer electron shells are full. For 10 points, name this group of gases such as the one in neon signs.

The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of this process, which takes place in chloroplasts. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes and use chlorophyll. For 10 points, name this process by which plants convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose.

This scientist discovered polonium, which she named for her native Poland, and radium. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, sharing it with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911. For 10 points, name this pioneer of radioactivity.

The boundary of this object is called the event horizon, and nothing inside it can escape, not even light. Stephen Hawking predicted that it should slowly lose mass through radiation. For 10 points, name this object, such as Sagittarius A*, with a singularity at its center.

The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a boundary where new crust forms in this theory, and the San Andreas Fault is a boundary where plates slide past each other. Subduction zones surround the Pacific in the so-called Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into moving slabs.

This English physician noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed to be protected from smallpox. In 1796 he inoculated a boy named James Phipps. For 10 points, name this man who developed the first vaccine.

Leonardo of Pisa introduced this sequence to Europe in his book "Liber Abaci" using a problem about rabbits. Each term is the sum of the two before it, as in 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. For 10 points, name this sequence, whose ratios approach the golden ratio.

This man helped break the Enigma code at Bletchley Park during World War II. He proposed an abstract machine now named for him and a test of whether a machine can imitate a human. For 10 points, name this British mathematician and computer scientist.

This composer, nicknamed "the Red Priest," taught at a Venetian orphanage for girls called the Ospedale della Pietà. He wrote hundreds of concertos, including a set of four violin concertos named for the times of the year. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer of "The Four Seasons."

This Dutch painter's "The Night Watch" depicts a militia company, and his "The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp" shows a dissection. He made many self-portraits and was known for dramatic contrasts of light and dark. For 10 points, name this artist of the Dutch Golden Age.

The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned this building as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It stands on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra and is made of white marble with four minarets. For 10 points, name this mausoleum, one of India's most famous landmarks.

This Spanish painter was a leader of Surrealism and sported an upturned mustache. His works include "The Persistence of Memory," which has melting clocks, and "Swans Reflecting Elephants." For 10 points, name this artist.

In Egyptian mythology, his brother Set tricked him into a coffin and later cut his body into pieces, which his wife Isis gathered. He became lord of the underworld, and their son Horus avenged him. For 10 points, name this Egyptian god of the dead.

This German monk is said to have nailed his 95 Theses to the door of the Wittenberg church in 1517. He was condemned at the Diet of Worms in 1521 and later translated the Bible into German. For 10 points, name this leader of the Protestant Reformation.

This man founded a school called the Lyceum and wrote the "Nicomachean Ethics" and the "Poetics." He was a student of Plato and tutor to Alexander the Great. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who developed formal logic.

Simon Kuznets developed the national accounts that led to this measure. It is computed by adding consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. For 10 points, name this measure of the value of a country's output, abbreviated GDP.

This Swiss psychologist proposed four stages of cognitive development: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational. He studied his own children and developed the idea of object permanence. For 10 points, name this child psychologist.

This river begins in the Andes of Peru and flows across Brazil past the city of Manaus. It discharges more water than any other river and is surrounded by the world's largest rainforest. For 10 points, name this South American river.

Lake Itasca in Minnesota is the source of this river. The Missouri and Ohio rivers are its major tributaries, and it empties into the Gulf of Mexico south of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this river that forms the boundary of many states.

text: This novel takes place on June 16, 1904, a date now celebrated as Bloomsday. Its chapters loosely parallel the episodes of the Odyssey, and its Dublin wanderers include the advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom and the young teacher Stephen Dedalus. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel, whose title is the Latin name of its mythic model.

Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are sent to spy on the title character of this play, who later holds a skull and recalls the jester Yorick. A play-within-a-play called "The Mousetrap" is staged to "catch the conscience of the King." For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy that includes the line "To be, or not to be."

This author's only novel published in his lifetime has a narrator who lives in a basement lit by 1,369 light bulbs. The narrator is told by a Brotherhood that he can serve as a spokesman, but he finally retreats underground. For 10 points, name this author of "Invisible Man."

In this Old English poem, a hero cuts off the arm of Grendel in the hall Heorot. He later kills Grendel's mother in an underwater lair, and in old age he dies fighting a dragon. For 10 points, name this epic whose title character is a Geat prince.

Mr. Lockwood narrates part of this novel, in which Nelly Dean tells of the Earnshaw family. A foundling named Heathcliff loves Catherine, who marries Edgar Linton at the neighboring Thrushcross Grange. For 10 points, name this novel set on the Yorkshire moors by Emily Brontë.

This author wrote of a man who is turned into a giant insect in a novella called "The Metamorphosis." His novels "The Trial" and "The Castle" feature characters trapped in baffling bureaucracies. For 10 points, name this Prague-born writer whose last name has become an adjective for nightmarish systems.

The crew of the Pequod includes the harpooneer Queequeg and the mate Starbuck. Its captain loses a leg to the title creature and swears vengeance, but the ship is destroyed, and only Ishmael survives. For 10 points, name this Herman Melville novel about a white whale.

Article 231 of this 1919 agreement made Germany accept responsibility for the war. It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors and limited the German army to 100,000 men. For 10 points, name this treaty that formally ended World War I with Germany.

Thucydides wrote the history of this conflict, in which he included Pericles' funeral oration. It included a disastrous Athenian expedition to Sicily and ended with the fall of Athens in 404 BC. For 10 points, name this war between Athens and Sparta.

This statesman edited the Ems Dispatch to provoke France into war in 1870. He practiced "Realpolitik" and oversaw the unification of Germany under Prussia. For 10 points, name this first chancellor of the German Empire, the "Iron Chancellor."

Toussaint Louverture led a slave uprising in Saint-Domingue that grew into this event. After his capture by the French, Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence in 1804. For 10 points, name this revolution that created the first Black republic in the Americas.

The Freedmen's Bureau was created during this period, which also saw the passage of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. It ended after the Compromise of 1877 led to the withdrawal of federal troops from the South. For 10 points, name this period after the Civil War.

Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 helped end the isolation that led to this event. In 1868 power was restored to the emperor, and the country rapidly industrialized and built a modern army. For 10 points, name this transformation of Japan named for the "enlightened rule" of Emperor Mutsuhito.

Mehmed II captured Constantinople for this state in 1453. Under Suleiman the Magnificent it besieged Vienna, and its elite infantry were called Janissaries. For 10 points, name this empire centered in Istanbul that lasted until 1922.

This scientist's equation describes how the wave function of a quantum system changes with time. He devised a thought experiment in which a cat in a sealed box is both alive and dead until observed. For 10 points, name this Austrian physicist.

In eukaryotes, this series of reactions occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, where acetyl-CoA is oxidized and NADH and FADH2 are produced. It is named for the biochemist Hans Krebs. For 10 points, name this cycle, also called the citric acid cycle.

This principle was proposed by Werner Heisenberg in 1927. It states that certain pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum, cannot both be known precisely at the same time. For 10 points, name this principle of quantum mechanics.

This principle says that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change. Adding more reactant, for example, shifts the reaction toward products. For 10 points, name this principle of chemical equilibrium named for a French chemist.

This astronomer used Cepheid variable stars to show that the Andromeda "nebula" lies outside the Milky Way. He found that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. For 10 points, name this American astronomer for whom a space telescope is named.

This Swiss mathematician solved the Königsberg bridge problem, founding graph theory, and solved the Basel problem. He introduced the notation f(x) and popularized the symbols e and i. For 10 points, name this prolific mathematician.

Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing a method of editing genes named for these repeating DNA sequences. It uses a guide RNA and the enzyme Cas9 to cut DNA at a chosen site. For 10 points, give this acronym for a gene-editing tool.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN was used to find this particle in 2012. Its associated field gives other elementary particles their mass. For 10 points, name this boson predicted by Peter Higgs and others.

The premiere of this composer's "The Rite of Spring" in 1913 in Paris is said to have caused a riot. He also wrote the ballets "The Firebird" and "Petrushka" for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. For 10 points, name this Russian composer.

This Mexican painter created many self-portraits, including ones with a necklace of thorns and a wounded deer. She was married to the muralist Diego Rivera and lived in the Blue House in Coyoacán. For 10 points, name this artist of "The Two Fridas."

Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque developed this movement, which broke objects into geometric facets seen from several angles at once. "Les Demoiselles d'Avignon" is often seen as a precursor, and its two phases are called analytic and synthetic. For 10 points, name this early 20th-century art movement.

This Austrian painter was a founder of the Vienna Secession and used gold leaf in his "Golden Phase." His works include "Judith and the Head of Holofernes" and a painting of two lovers embracing. For 10 points, name this artist of "The Kiss."

In this Hindu scripture, a warrior hesitates to fight on the field of Kurukshetra. His charioteer, who is an avatar of Vishnu, teaches him about duty and devotion. For 10 points, name this part of the Mahabharata, a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna.

In this Mesopotamian epic, a king of Uruk befriends the wild man Enkidu and fights the monster Humbaba. After Enkidu dies, the king seeks out Utnapishtim to learn the secret of immortality. For 10 points, name this epic of the Babylonians and Sumerians, named for its hero.

This philosopher wrote the "Critique of Pure Reason" and spent his life in Königsberg. He argued that one should act only according to a maxim that one could will to be a universal law. For 10 points, name this German thinker who formulated the categorical imperative.

This thinker wrote "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" and introduced the idea of the Übermensch. His works "Beyond Good and Evil" and "The Gay Science" include the declaration that "God is dead." For 10 points, name this German philosopher.

This thinker collaborated with Friedrich Engels on "The Communist Manifesto" in 1848. His multivolume "Das Kapital" analyzed capitalism through concepts such as surplus value. For 10 points, name this German philosopher and economist.

This British economist argued in "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money" that governments should use deficit spending to fight depressions. He was a delegate at the Bretton Woods conference. For 10 points, name this namesake of an economic school.

This American linguist wrote "Syntactic Structures" in 1957. He proposed that humans have an innate capacity for language, often called universal grammar. For 10 points, name this MIT professor and political critic.

Ferdinand de Lesseps oversaw the construction of this waterway, which opened in 1869. It links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and spares ships a trip around Africa. For 10 points, name this Egyptian canal.

This lake in Siberia is the deepest in the world, at over 5,000 feet. It holds about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water and is home to the freshwater Baikal seal. For 10 points, name this Russian lake.
